opus-5.5.text:
I think Noam is largely right, though I'd put it a little differently than he sometimes does.

The core of his point is that these systems are not theories of anything. They're incredible at mimicry, at absorbing vast amounts of text and producing statistically plausible continuations. But a model that can produce English sentences is not the same thing as an explanation of why human languages have the properties they do. Noam has always been interested in the question of why language is the way it is: why certain structures show up across languages and others never do, why children converge on grammars from relatively little data. Large language models don't answer those questions. They just sidestep them.

One of the most telling things is the data. A child acquires language from maybe tens of millions of words, a lot of it messy, a lot of it not even directed at them. These models are trained on trillions of tokens, orders of magnitude more than any human will ever hear in a lifetime. So whatever they're doing, it's not obviously what children are doing. If anything, the success of these systems with that much data is a kind of indirect argument that humans must bring something else to the table: some innate structure, some prior constraints. That's essentially Noam's poverty-of-the-stimulus argument, and I don't think LLMs refute it at all.

There's also the "impossible languages" point he and others have made. If you train these systems on languages that violate the kinds of structural principles human languages obey, things based on linear order rather than hierarchical structure, they can often learn them more or less just as well. Humans can't, or at least not as natural languages. A theory of human language ought to tell you what's possible and what's not. A system that will learn almost anything isn't telling you much about the specific thing humans do.

Where I'd add my own spin is on the meaning side. Noam has focused a lot on syntax, and I've focused more on the fact that these systems don't really have models of the world. They don't have stable representations of entities, events, and their relations that they reason over. That's why you get hallucinations, why you get these weird failures of compositionality, why you can get a system to say a thing and its negation in the same conversation. Human language is a way of mapping thought onto sound or text, and these systems have the text without the thought. So they're an interesting artifact, and as engineering they're impressive in certain ways, but as science of language? I think they've taught us surprisingly little.

Now, to be fair, I'd say they've taught us *something*. They've shown that you can get a lot further on surface fluency with pure distributional statistics than many people would have guessed twenty years ago. That's a genuine empirical finding. But it's a finding about how far you can push statistics, not about how the human mind works. And I think people have very badly conflated those two things.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts children acquiring language from “maybe tens of millions of words” with models trained on “trillions of tokens,” describing the models’ training text as vast.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Noam is largely right, though I'd put it a little differently than he does. His point is that these systems can learn any language, including impossible languages that no child could acquire and that violate the constraints we see across every human language. A theory that fits everything explains nothing. If your system learns the possible and the impossible with equal ease, it isn't telling you what's special about the human faculty.

Where I'd add nuance is that LLMs have taught us something, just not what their proponents claim. They've taught us that an enormous amount of surface structure can be extracted from statistical regularities given trillions of tokens. That's a genuine finding. But kids don't get trillions of tokens. They get maybe tens of millions of words by the time they're a few years old, and they get them in a world full of reference, intention, and interaction. So the systems are solving a different problem under radically different conditions, and that makes them a poor model of acquisition.

The other thing I'd say, and this is my old refrain, is that language isn't just distributional statistics. It's about compositionality and about meaning, about mapping sentences onto a model of the world. These systems still struggle with exactly that. They're fluent, but fluency and understanding are not the same thing. So when people say LLMs have refuted Chomsky, they're confusing a tremendous engineering achievement with a scientific account of how humans do it. Those are two different questions, and I think history will show that the second one is still wide open.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts LLMs learning from trillions of tokens with young children hearing only tens of millions of words, clearly communicating the difference in linguistic exposure.

astra-6.text:
I think he’s largely right, but I would put it a little differently. Large language models have taught us something about how much you can do by learning statistical patterns from enormous amounts of text. That’s interesting, and we shouldn’t dismiss it. But it doesn’t follow that we’ve explained how human language works.

There are really two questions here: Can you build a system that produces convincing language? And have you identified the mechanisms by which a child learns language? Success on the first question doesn’t settle the second. Children learn under very different conditions, with much less linguistic input, but with perception, action, and social interaction.

Where I would push back on Chomsky is that the success of these systems ought to constrain our arguments. If we thought a particular kind of performance was impossible without explicit grammatical machinery, then we should revisit that claim. But we also have to look beyond fluent output: Does the system generalize reliably? Does it preserve meaning when you change the circumstances? What explains its failures?

So I wouldn’t say we’ve learned nothing. I’d say we’ve learned a great deal about generating language, and considerably less about the human capacity for language. Those are different achievements.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts LLMs learning from “enormous amounts of text” with children learning from “much less linguistic input.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think he's largely right if the question is whether these systems explain how human language works. You can build a system that produces very fluent language without showing that children learn in anything like the same way. Children acquire language from far less data, and they connect it to their understanding of the world, their intentions, and their interactions with other people.

Where I would qualify the claim is that large language models have shown us that you can get more out of statistical learning than many people expected. That's an interesting result, and theories of language ought to take it seriously. But success at predicting words doesn't, by itself, settle questions about innate structure, compositionality, or how people represent meaning.

The crucial thing is to turn these systems into testable hypotheses about human cognition. Do they make the same errors people make? Do they learn the same things from comparable experience? Fluency alone isn't enough to establish that we've explained language.

r001.rationale: The response says children acquire language from far less data, but it does not state that large language models rely on an internet-scale corpus, so the full contrast is missing.
